fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some notes added (most probably by K. D. MacDonald?). See below for details.]

item.description: to cease as in a lull after a period of wind, rain.
same as above [i.e. abhsadh (q.v.)].
five speed gear.
turmoil, disorder.
unsteady or clumsy with your feet.
a lazy fellow, prone to daydreaming and not making much effort to succeed in life. [NOTES: note added above ‘amasgaidh’ – am + easgaidh?]
breath. “Cha robh anathadh ann.” [NOTES: note added – anfhadh?]
on the top of a wall in the old thatched house. This describes the top of the inside wall.
this refers to the outside wall at the top of a wall [sic]. [NOTES: ‘fraigh’ corrected to ‘fràigh’.]
neighbouring area, community.
a stake to which a tether was tied. This stake was driven into the ground to prevent the animals’ escape.
a sarcastic, witty person. A person who was likely [to] cut you off with a quick remark. [NOTES: ‘beumal’ corrected to ‘beumail’.]
applied to a mischievous child. Have heard a woman in my own village refer to her two sons as ‘biodagan beag’ is ‘biodagan mór’; not just as youngsters but in the rowdier teenage years.
catch the thief. A game played by the informant in his younger years.
applied to someone of great fame and repute.
periwig.
a morsel, a small bit of cheese or other commodity.
phosphorescence.
creel straps. [Cf. iris.]
also used to mean creel straps. [Cf. iorsnan.]
as in: “Cha robh blàth aige sin air an rud a thainig as a dheidh.” The [sic] seems to mean to have an effect on something.
applied to a sneaky, thieving person.
commotion, consternation. [NOTES: ‘gug’ corrected to ‘gùg’.]
to flit both in the general sense of the word and as in flitting to a new house.
to grimace with pain.
applied to a person with noticeably thick lips.
a sickle-shaped instrument used to catch sand eels.
dirty, contaminated water.
the thick, rubbery fat left at the bottom of a pan after melting.
a parcel.
a variant form of ‘giogladh’ meaning to tickle.
would be applied to a skilled craftsman. Not sure of the exact craft.
a temperamental man likely to snap at the slightest intimidation.
Bha crùib anns an rathad. – a bend.
a very old woman or alternately an old instrument about to fall apart. [NOTES: ‘chruilleasg’ corrected to ‘chrùilleasg’.]
tricks, wiles. “Nach uamhasach na cuiraidean a bh’aig an duine sin.”
getting drunk on someone else’s whisky.
Cha d’fhuair sinn deargadh eisg. – ‘deargadh’ refers to a very small catch of fish.
to fend someone or something off. [NOTES: corrected to ‘diùchairt’.]
surface peat which is dry and which can be used immediately on a fire.
bottom layer of peat? Not sure of this.
a loud blow, e.g. a boat crashing on rocks. “Nach i a fhuair am faghar.”
in context of someone dancing and referring to the quick movement of the feet and hands. Also applied in everyday life when someone puts him/herself in a humorous physical position.
an account of an incident; a report.
to make a croaking sound, e.g. if someone was suffering from a cold.
to have a preference; to favour one person over another. [NOTES: note added – a’ gabhail fàmas dha.]
nowadays would be applied to a barman or waiter.
crashing, roaring sound of waves.
tittle tattle; gossip.
to kick.
a person who suffered from a weakness in the knee joints.
informant is not sure of this but thinks he has heard this in the context of referring to a member of the fairer sex.
a wide gap, opening.
lung.
a discarded item of clothing left to rot outside in the rain.
a grace note.
a reef which lessened the sail in high winds.
a rat’s nest.
in fragments.
